introduction-the-paradox-of-safety.core: Studying only failures is like studying only broken cars. Most of the time complex systems work because people constantly adapt. To improve safety you also need to understand why things normally go right.

first_principles.problem: Reliability work focuses entirely on rare incidents and misses the everyday adaptations that prevent thousands more.
truths: The same adaptive behaviours cause both.

analogy.title: A mechanic who only sees broken cars
analogy.story: They'd never learn how good drivers keep cars healthy for 200,000 miles.
analogy.breaks: Failures still matter, and Safety II adds to incident analysis rather than replacing it.

example.title: A routine week
flow: Safety II also asks why 498 succeeded

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The hidden success factor is preserved and formalised.

example.outcome: you learn from the normal as well as the broken.

check.q: Why study successful operations, not just failures?
check.a: Success is far more common and reveals the adaptations that actually keep systems safe.

safety-i-vs-safety-ii-the-core-differenc.core: Safety I assumes the system is correct and humans are the liability, so it constrains and blames people. Safety II sees humans as the source of resilience, adapting to gaps the design didn't anticipate, so it supports and learns from them.

first_principles.problem: Treating people as the weak link leads to more rules and blame, which reduces the adaptive capacity that prevents failures.
derivation: **Safety I**: prevent deviation, more procedures, blame errors.

analogy.title: Seeing employees as risks vs. assets
analogy.story: One company adds more rules after mistakes; the other asks how staff usually manage to save the day.
analogy.breaks: Some hard constraints, such as safety interlocks, are still essential.

example.title: After a near-outage
flow: Safety I: add approval step, reprimand
Safety II: interview how on-call noticed early
Build their ad-hoc check into a dashboard

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Adaptive capacity grows instead of shrinking.

example.outcome: a culture that strengthens human resilience.

check.q: How does Safety II view human performance variability?
check.a: As a source of resilience that lets people adapt to conditions the design didn't anticipate.

work-as-imagined-vs-work-as-done.core: The gap between how procedures say work happens and how it actually happens is where Safety II looks. That gap holds the tacit knowledge, workarounds and adaptations that keep things running, and the risks too.

first_principles.problem: Leaders design processes from the imagined view and don't see why real work deviates, so improvements miss reality.
truths: Gaps contain both risk and wisdom.
derivation: **Classify** them: useful adaptations vs risky shortcuts.
**Update** processes and tools to match good practice.

analogy.title: A city's planned paths vs. desire paths
analogy.story: Planners pave sidewalks; people walk diagonal desire paths across the grass. Smart planners pave the desire paths.
analogy.breaks: Not every desire path is safe, so evaluate before formalising.

example.title: A database maintenance procedure
flow: Real: DBAs check replication lag first, manually

check.q: What are 'desire paths' an analogy for?
check.a: The adaptations people actually make in work-as-done that differ from official procedures.

success-analysis-studying-the-near-miss-.core: Success analysis treats near misses ('almost an incident') and quiet wins ('that went well despite difficulty') as learning events. Run short reviews of what helped, then reinforce those capacities: monitoring, skills, slack, collaboration.

first_principles.problem: Near misses are forgotten because nothing broke, and the lessons they hold are lost until a real failure occurs.
truths: Near misses share causes with incidents.
Learning from them is low-stakes and frequent.
derivation: **Capture** near misses and wins (a lightweight form, Slack).
Run **'learning reviews'**: what made this go right?
**Identify** protective factors (a person, a dashboard, slack time).

analogy.title: Aviation near-miss reporting
analogy.story: Pilots report close calls, and those reports improve safety more than crash investigations alone.
analogy.breaks: Reviews need psychological safety, or people won't report near misses.

example.title: A quiet-win review
flow: Pre-scaling playbook, war-room rota, capacity tests
example.outcome: learning from the many events where things went right.

check.q: What question drives a Safety II learning review?
check.a: 'What made this go right (or not go wrong), and how do we strengthen it?'
